summary: This document defines a mechanism for preserving the Frame Check Sequence through Ethernet, Frame Relay, HDLC and PPP pseudowires, rather than stripping it at the edge of the tunnel.

eli5.summary: Each frame carries a checksum, like a seal. Normally it is thrown away when the frame enters a tunnel. This keeps the seal so it can still be checked at the other end.

questions: why retain the fcs in a pseudowire
how is fcs retention signaled in l2tpv3
what is the fcs retention indicator
subtitle: Lets a pseudowire carry the original frame checksum end to end, so corruption inside the provider network can be detected.

tldr.problem: Pseudowire encapsulations remove the original Frame Check Sequence at the ingress edge and regenerate it at the egress edge, so corruption inside the provider network passes unnoticed through Layer 2 switches.
tldr.mechanism: The egress PE asks for the original FCS to be kept, using a Pseudowire Interface Parameter sub-TLV (0x0A) for MPLS-based pseudowires or the FCS Retention AVP (type 92) for L2TPv3-based ones.
tldr.outcome: Retention only happens when both ends ask for it with the same FCS length, at the cost of 2 or 4 extra octets per packet. Without it, the old remove-and-regenerate behavior remains the default.

today: RFC 4720 is a Proposed Standard from November 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why the FCS Gets Lost
sections.content:
The specifications for Ethernet, Frame Relay, HDLC and PPP pseudowires all say that the original Frame Check Sequence (FCS) is removed at the ingress Provider Edge (PE) and regenerated at the egress PE. That means a frame can be altered on the way through the pseudowire and nobody can tell.

The RFC points out that this is not only about PW-aware devices. ANY LSR or router on the path can corrupt the encapsulated payload. Because the FCS is calculated on network egress, the corruption passes transparently through ALL Layer 2 switches (Ethernet and Frame Relay). Only at the endpoint can the packet be discarded, and depending on its contents the corruption may never be detected.

Calculating the FCS on questionable data also subverts the error checking already in place in service provider and customer networks.
sections.eli5: Imagine a letter with a wax seal. If the post office rips off the seal at the start and makes a new one at the end, a smudge in the middle is never noticed. The new seal looks fine even if the letter was damaged.

sections.title: What the Mechanism Does
sections.content:
The document lets the ingress PE retain the original frame FCS and relieves the egress PE of regenerating it. It is an OPTIONAL mechanism. For interoperability with systems that do not implement it, the default stays the same: the FCS is removed at ingress and regenerated at egress.

It may be used only with Ethernet pseudowires in raw mode, Frame Relay pseudowires in port mode, and HDLC and PPP pseudowires.

It does not carry errored frames. The FCS MUST still be examined at the ingress PE and errored frames MUST be discarded. The egress PE MAY also examine the FCS, and if it does, errored frames MUST be discarded. It MAY also raise an alarm or count them.
sections.eli5: Both ends can agree to keep the original seal on the letter. But a letter that was already damaged when it arrived at the first post office is still thrown away right there.

sections.title: Signaling with MPLS-Based Pseudowires
sections.content:
With the signaling procedures of RFC 4447, a Pseudowire Interface Parameter Sub-TLV signals the wish to retain the FCS when a VC label is advertised. It has type 0x0A, length 4, and is called the FCS Retention Indicator.

Its presence means the egress PE requests retention. It does not obligate the ingress PE; it only indicates that the ingress PE MAY retain the FCS. The sender MUST NOT retain the FCS if the parameter is not present in the VC FEC element.

The parameter holds a 16-bit FCS length. For Ethernet this is always 4. For HDLC, PPP and Frame Relay it is 2 or 4. Since FCS length is a local setting on those interfaces, retention only makes sense when both ends use the same length.

Unknown parameters are silently ignored, so older systems stay compatible. The FCS is retained ONLY if the indicator with an identical FCS length appears in the advertisements for both directions. An ingress PE that does not want retention just sends its own label mapping for the opposite direction without the indicator, which prevents retention in either direction.

Without PWE3 signaling, whether to retain the FCS MUST be provisioned identically on both PEs. If provisioning support is missing, the default is to remove the FCS.
sections.eli5: When the two ends set up their tunnel, each says whether it wants to keep the seal and what size it is. The seal is only kept if both say yes and agree on the size. If one says nothing, the old way is used.

sections.title: Signaling with L2TPv3-Based Pseudowires
sections.content:
With the L2TPv3 procedures of RFC 3931, the FCS Retention AVP is used, Attribute Type 92. Its value is a single 2-octet unsigned integer, the FCS Length, with the same meaning and values (4 for Ethernet, 2 or 4 for HDLC, PPP and Frame Relay) as in the MPLS case.

The AVP in an ICRQ or ICRP message means an LCCE (PE) asks its peer to retain the FCS for the session being established. A receiving LCCE that recognizes the AVP and complies MUST include an FCS Retention AVP as acknowledgement in a corresponding ICRP or ICCN message. Retention is always bidirectional, so the FCS is retained only if both LCCEs send the AVP during session establishment.

The AVP Length is 8, the M bit MUST be 0, and the AVP MAY be hidden (the H bit MAY be 1 or 0).
sections.eli5: It is the same handshake in a different tunnel system. One side asks, the other side must answer with the same request if it agrees, and the seal is kept only if both have asked.

sections.title: Integrity, Cost and Applicability
sections.content:
Keeping the original FCS, generated by the Customer Edge (CE), improves data integrity. If the payload passes the FCS check at the destination CE, it was not altered in transit, at least to the accuracy of the original FCS. The price is the extra overhead, generally 2 or 4 octets per payload packet. The signaling is backward compatible with systems that do not implement it.

The applicability statement says retention is not needed where inner payloads have their own error checking, such as TCP. It can be valuable for payloads that rely on link-layer error detection, such as SNA. It also lets pseudowires meet the requirement that media interconnecting 802.1 bridges have at least 32-bit FCS protection.

It is one option among others, such as end-to-end IPsec between the PEs or internal integrity mechanisms in the P routers. The RFC notes that a mechanism STRONGER than the source CE's FCS may be wasteful.
sections.eli5: Keeping the seal costs a little extra paper on every letter. It matters most for letters that have no other way of showing damage, and matters less for letters that can check themselves.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
The document creates no new registries. The FCS Retention Indicator interface parameter was already allocated by RFC 4446, so no further IANA action is needed for the MPLS side.

For L2TP, IANA assigned one value in the "Control Message Attribute Value Pairs" section as per RFC 3438. The new AVP is 92, listed in the IANA L2TP parameters registry as "FCS Retention".
sections.eli5: The number for the new option was reserved in the official list of numbers, so nobody else will use it for something different.

fields.name: FCS Length
fields.desc: Length of the original FCS being retained; a 2-octet unsigned integer.

cells: ICRQ or ICRP, acknowledged in ICRP or ICCN
